title: What is the first appearance of Superman?
answer: Superman first appeared in Action Comics #1, cover-dated June 1938 and on sale in April 1938, created by writer Jerry Siegel and artist Joe Shuster and published by Detective Comics, Inc., the company that became DC Comics. It is the first superhero comic and the most valuable comic book in the world: a CGC 8.5 copy sold for 6 million dollars in April 2024.
body:
## The issue

Action Comics #1 was a 64-page anthology priced at ten cents. Superman's 13-page story, adapted from a strip Siegel and Shuster had failed to sell to newspaper syndicates for years, opens with the baby rocketed from a dying planet and ends with him carrying a car over his head — the image on Shuster's cover. The other features in the issue (Zatara, Tex Thomson, Scoop Scanlon) are footnotes now.

Superman did not appear on the cover again until Action Comics #7; the publisher was unsure the character was the reason the book sold until newsstand surveys said so.

## What followed

- **Superman #1** (Summer 1939) — the first comic book devoted to a single superhero and the second most valuable comic: a CGC 7.0 copy sold privately for 5.3 million dollars in 2022.
- **Action Comics** has been published continuously since; issue #1000 appeared in April 2018.

## Collecting Action Comics #1

Surviving copies are commonly estimated at around a hundred, most in low grade. The copies that set records — 3.25 million dollars for a CGC 8.5 in April 2021 and 6 million dollars for a different CGC 8.5 in April 2024, both at public auction — are the finest known. Restored copies, incomplete copies and even covers alone trade for large sums.

Beware of reprints: DC has issued facsimiles and the 1974 Famous First Edition oversized reprint, and the 1938 issue has been counterfeited. Any copy offered as an original should be graded by CGC or CBCS or examined by a specialist. See [What is a facsimile edition?](/guides/what-is-a-facsimile-edition).

## Superman in the Golden Age

Early Superman keys after Action #1 include Superman #1 (1939), Action Comics #23 (April 1940, first Lex Luthor), and Superman #14 (1942, the patriotic shield cover). Our [Golden Age collection](/collections/golden-age) lists what is currently available, and the [Superman character page](/characters/superman) collects everything on this site about him.

sources.label: Heritage Auctions — Action Comics #1 sale, April 2024

title: What is the first appearance of Batman?
answer: Batman first appeared in Detective Comics #27, cover-dated May 1939, in a six-page story titled “The Case of the Chemical Syndicate”, created by Bob Kane and Bill Finger and published by Detective Comics, Inc. (DC). Finger, who wrote the story and shaped the costume, was officially credited by DC as co-creator from 2015. A CGC 8.0 copy sold for 1.5 million dollars at Heritage Auctions in January 2022.
body:
## The issue

Detective Comics had been running as a crime anthology since March 1937. Issue #27 introduced "the Bat-Man", a caped detective in a story that already has Commissioner Gordon and Bruce Wayne. Kane drew the cover of Batman swinging across a rooftop with a criminal under his arm. There is no Robin, no Joker and no Batmobile yet.

## The keys that follow

- **Detective Comics #29–#31** — early covers and the first Batarang and Batgyro (#31, September 1939).
- **Detective Comics #33** (November 1939) — Batman's origin told for the first time.
- **Detective Comics #38** (April 1940) — first appearance of Robin.
- **Batman #1** (Spring 1940) — first appearances of the Joker and Catwoman; a CGC 9.4 copy sold for 2.22 million dollars in January 2021.

## Collecting Detective Comics #27

It is the second most important Golden Age key after Action Comics #1 and, like it, survives mostly in low grade. Copies in any complete condition trade for six figures and above. Reprints exist, including a 1974 Famous First Edition and later facsimiles; grade or authenticate any copy offered as original.

## Why Bill Finger's credit matters to collectors

For decades the byline read "Batman created by Bob Kane". After a campaign by Finger's family and historians, DC changed the credit to "Bob Kane with Bill Finger" in 2015, beginning with the Batman television and film credits that autumn. Labels and listings now generally name both.

The [Batman character page](/characters/batman) collects Batman books currently in the store, including Modern Age keys such as [Batman Adventures #12](/guides/batman-adventures-12-first-harley-quinn).

title: What is the first appearance of Captain America?
answer: Captain America first appeared in Captain America Comics #1, cover-dated March 1941 and on sale in December 1940, created by Joe Simon and Jack Kirby for Timely Comics, the company that became Marvel. The issue is famous for its cover of Cap punching Adolf Hitler, published a year before the United States entered the Second World War, and it also introduced Bucky and the Red Skull. A CGC 9.4 copy sold for 3.12 million dollars at Heritage Auctions in April 2022.
body:
## The issue

Unlike most Golden Age heroes, Captain America debuted in his own title rather than in an anthology. Simon and Kirby produced the whole issue: the origin of Steve Rogers, the super-soldier serum and Bucky Barnes, and the first Red Skull (in this issue a Nazi agent named George Maxon). The Hitler cover was controversial enough to draw threats to the publisher's office.

## What followed

Captain America Comics ran for 75 issues to 1950 (with a brief 1954 revival as Captain America... Commie Smasher). The character was revived in the Silver Age in Avengers #4 (March 1964) — see [Avengers #4 explained](/guides/avengers-4-captain-america-returns) — and has been published continuously since, in Tales of Suspense from #59 and in his own title from 1968.

## Collecting Captain America Comics #1

One of the three or four most valuable Golden Age books, alongside Action Comics #1, Detective Comics #27 and Marvel Comics #1. High-grade copies are exceptionally rare; the 9.4 sold in 2022 is among the finest known. Mid- and low-grade copies still trade well into six figures. Restored copies are common and must be priced as such.

## Related keys

- **Captain America Comics #3** (May 1941) — Stan Lee's first published work, a text story.
- **Avengers #4** (March 1964) — Silver Age return.
- **Captain America #100** (April 1968) — first issue of the solo title, continuing Tales of Suspense numbering.

See the [Captain America character page](/characters/captain-america) for what is in the store, and the [Timely Comics publisher page](/publishers/timely-comics) for other Golden Age Marvel.

title: What is the first appearance of Captain Marvel (Shazam)?
answer: The original Captain Marvel — Billy Batson, who says “Shazam!” — first appeared in Whiz Comics #2, cover-dated February 1940, created by writer Bill Parker and artist C. C. Beck for Fawcett Publications. The issue is numbered #2 on the cover because Fawcett had prepared unpublished ashcan editions as #1; there is no regular Whiz Comics #1. During the 1940s Captain Marvel outsold Superman.
body:
## The issue

Whiz Comics #2 introduced Billy Batson, the wizard Shazam and the transformation into Captain Marvel, in a story by Parker with Beck's clean, cartoon-influenced art. The same issue introduced Spy Smasher, Ibis the Invincible and Golden Arrow. Because of the ashcan numbering, the issue is sometimes listed as Whiz Comics #1 (#2).

## The Fawcett years

Captain Marvel became the best-selling comic character of the 1940s, with Captain Marvel Adventures reaching bi-weekly publication. The Marvel Family grew to include Captain Marvel Jr. (Whiz Comics #25, December 1941) and Mary Marvel (Captain Marvel Adventures #18, December 1942). DC (then National) sued Fawcett for copyright infringement in 1941; after years of litigation Fawcett settled in 1953 and stopped publishing the character.

## The DC era

DC licensed the character in 1972 and published Shazam! #1 in February 1973, using "Shazam!" as the title because Marvel Comics had trademarked the name Captain Marvel for its own character in 1967. DC later bought the Fawcett characters outright, and since 2011 the character himself has been called Shazam.

## Collecting

Whiz Comics #2 is one of the great Golden Age keys, scarce in any grade. Other Fawcett keys include Captain Marvel Adventures #1 (1941, drawn by Jack Kirby), Whiz Comics #25 and Master Comics #21 (Captain Marvel Jr.), and Wow Comics #9 (Mary Marvel's first cover, 1943). See the [Fawcett Publications publisher page](/publishers/fawcett-publications) and the [character page](/characters/captain-marvel-shazam).

title: What is the first appearance of Wonder Woman?
answer: Wonder Woman first appeared in All Star Comics #8, cover-dated December 1941 – January 1942, in a nine-page origin story by William Moulton Marston (writing as Charles Moulton) and artist H. G. Peter, published by All-American Publications, one of the companies that merged into DC. Her first cover appearance and first regular feature followed in Sensation Comics #1 (January 1942), and her own title began with Wonder Woman #1 in Summer 1942.
body:
## The debut

All Star Comics was the home of the Justice Society of America. Issue #8 added a backup story introducing Princess Diana of Paradise Island, Steve Trevor and the contest that sends Diana to "man's world". Marston, a psychologist who had helped develop an early lie detector, created the character explicitly as a female hero for girls and boys alike; Peter's art defined her look for the next two decades.

## The three early keys

| Issue | Cover date | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| All Star Comics #8 | Dec 1941 – Jan 1942 | First appearance and origin |
| Sensation Comics #1 | January 1942 | First cover appearance; start of her regular feature |
| Wonder Woman #1 | Summer 1942 | First issue of her own title; expanded origin |

All Star Comics #8 is the most valuable of the three and one of the most valuable Golden Age books featuring a female character. Because she appears only in the backup, she is not on the cover.

## Later notes for collectors

- Wonder Woman is one of the few characters published continuously since the Golden Age.
- The New 52 Wonder Woman (2011) run by Brian Azzarello and Cliff Chiang is represented in the store by [issue #49](/store/wonder-woman-2011-49-cgc-9-8).

See the [Wonder Woman character page](/characters/wonder-woman) for what is available, and the [DC Comics publisher page](/publishers/dc-comics) for other Golden Age DC.

title: What is the first appearance of the Fantastic Four?
answer: The Fantastic Four first appeared in Fantastic Four #1, cover-dated November 1961, created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby for Marvel Comics. The issue introduced Reed Richards, Sue Storm, Johnny Storm and Ben Grimm, told their origin, and introduced the Mole Man as their first villain. It is regarded as the start of the “Marvel Age” of comics and is Marvel's most important Silver Age key after Amazing Fantasy #15.
body:
## The issue

According to Lee's often-told account, publisher Martin Goodman asked for a superhero team to compete with DC's Justice League of America, and Lee and Kirby produced a team that argued, had no secret identities and no costumes in the first issue. Kirby's cover shows the four battling a giant monster rising from the street. The Mole Man and his Monster Isle fill the second half of the book.

## Why it matters

Fantastic Four #1 established the tone of Marvel's 1960s — flawed heroes, continuity between titles, New York as the setting — and the Lee–Kirby run that followed (102 issues) introduced much of the Marvel Universe: Doctor Doom (#5), the Skrulls (#2), the Inhumans (#45), the Silver Surfer and Galactus (#48–50), and the Black Panther (#52).

## Collecting Fantastic Four #1

- High grades are very scarce; most copies are in the Good-to-Fine range.
- Complete low-grade copies remain expensive because demand is deep; a CGC 2.0 copy is a serious book, and one is [in the store](/store/fantastic-four-1-cgc-2-0).
- Reprints: Marvel Milestone Edition (1991), Golden Record reprint (1966, with a record), and recent facsimiles. Check the indicia and price.

## Related Fantastic Four keys in the store

- **Fantastic Four #18** (September 1963) — first appearance of the Super-Skrull. [See the listing](/store/fantastic-four-18-cgc-8-0).
- **Fantastic Four #48** (March 1966) — first Silver Surfer and Galactus. See [First appearance of the Silver Surfer](/guides/first-appearance-of-silver-surfer).
- **Fantastic Four #52** (July 1966) — first Black Panther. See [First appearance of Black Panther](/guides/first-appearance-of-black-panther).

The [Fantastic Four character page](/characters/fantastic-four) lists current stock.

title: What is the first appearance of the Hulk?
answer: The Hulk first appeared in The Incredible Hulk #1, cover-dated May 1962, created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby. In this first issue the Hulk is grey, not green — the colour was changed from issue #2 because the grey printed inconsistently. The issue also introduces Bruce Banner, Rick Jones, General Thaddeus “Thunderbolt” Ross and Betty Ross. The original series was cancelled after six issues.
body:
## The issue

Banner is caught in the gamma bomb test while saving teenager Rick Jones, and at nightfall becomes the grey Hulk. Kirby's cover shows the Hulk looming over Banner with the caption "Is he man or monster or… is he both?". The grey colouring was the plan; the printer could not keep it consistent, so Lee switched to green with issue #2 (July 1962).

## Cancellation and return

The Incredible Hulk ended with #6 (March 1963). The character guested in Fantastic Four #12 (March 1963, the first Hulk–Thing fight) and Avengers #1–3, then got a regular feature in Tales to Astonish from #60 (October 1964), which took over the Hulk's numbering as The Incredible Hulk #102 in April 1968. That is why the 1962 issues are #1–6 and the run then jumps to #102.

## Collecting Incredible Hulk #1

A top-tier Silver Age key: scarce in high grade, expensive in any grade, and frequently restored. Incredible Hulk #2 (first green Hulk) and #6 (last issue) are the next most collected of the original run.

## Other Hulk keys in the store

- **Incredible Hulk #181** (November 1974) — first full appearance of Wolverine, the Bronze Age's most valuable book. See [Why is Incredible Hulk #181 so valuable?](/guides/incredible-hulk-181-first-wolverine).
- **Savage She-Hulk #1** (February 1980) — first She-Hulk. See [First appearance of She-Hulk](/guides/first-appearance-of-she-hulk).

The [Hulk character page](/characters/hulk) lists current stock.

title: What is the first appearance of Spider-Man?
answer: Spider-Man first appeared in Amazing Fantasy #15, cover-dated August 1962, in an 11-page origin story by Stan Lee and Steve Ditko with a cover by Jack Kirby and Ditko. It was the final issue of the anthology. The Amazing Spider-Man #1 followed in March 1963. Amazing Fantasy #15 is the most valuable Silver Age comic: a CGC 9.6 copy sold for 3.6 million dollars at Heritage Auctions in September 2021.
body:
## The issue

Amazing Adult Fantasy, a Lee–Ditko science-fiction anthology, was being cancelled. Lee used the last issue, retitled Amazing Fantasy, to try a teenage hero with real problems. Peter Parker's origin — the spider bite, the wrestling match, the burglar, Uncle Ben's death and "with great power there must also come great responsibility" — is complete in those eleven pages. The rest of the issue is short Ditko fantasy stories.

## Why it is worth so much

Spider-Man became Marvel's flagship character with a global audience, the issue was a low-selling final issue of a cancelled anthology, and it appeared before the collector market existed, so high-grade copies are extraordinarily rare. The CGC census shows the top grades in single digits. Demand from every kind of collector and investor meets a tiny supply.

## Early Spider-Man keys

| Issue | Cover date | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Amazing Spider-Man #1 | March 1963 | First issue; first Chameleon and J. Jonah Jameson |
| Amazing Spider-Man #2 | May 1963 | First Vulture |
| Amazing Spider-Man #3 | July 1963 | First Doctor Octopus |
| Amazing Spider-Man #4 | September 1963 | First Sandman |
| Amazing Spider-Man #14 | July 1964 | First Green Goblin |

## Reprints to know

Amazing Fantasy #15 has been reprinted many times: Marvel Tales #1 (1964), Marvel Milestone Edition (1992), Golden Record reprint (1966), and modern facsimiles. See [What is a facsimile edition?](/guides/what-is-a-facsimile-edition).

## Spider-Man in the store

Silver and Bronze Age Amazing Spider-Man keys currently listed include [#8](/store/amazing-spider-man-8-cgc-8-0), [#102](/store/amazing-spider-man-102-cgc-9-4) and [#129](/store/amazing-spider-man-129-cbcs-8-5), the first Punisher. The [Spider-Man character page](/characters/spider-man) has everything.

title: What is the first appearance of Thor?
answer: Marvel's Thor first appeared in Journey into Mystery #83, cover-dated August 1962, in a story plotted by Stan Lee, scripted by Larry Lieber and drawn by Jack Kirby. Dr. Don Blake finds a walking stick in a Norwegian cave, strikes it, and becomes Thor. The Thor feature took over the anthology, and Journey into Mystery was renamed The Mighty Thor with issue #126 in March 1966.
body:
## The debut

Journey into Mystery had been a monster and fantasy anthology. Issue #83's lead story, "The Stone Men from Saturn", introduced Thor, Mjolnir and the inscription "Whosoever holds this hammer, if he be worthy, shall possess the power of Thor". Kirby's cover shows Thor smashing a stone giant.

## Early Thor keys

| Issue | Cover date | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Journey into Mystery #83 | August 1962 | First Thor |
| Journey into Mystery #84 | September 1962 | First Jane Foster (then Jane Nelson) |
| Journey into Mystery #85 | October 1962 | First Loki, Asgard, Odin and Heimdall |
| Journey into Mystery #97 | October 1963 | Start of the "Tales of Asgard" backups |
| Journey into Mystery Annual #1 | 1965 | First appearance of Hercules in the Marvel Universe |
| Journey into Mystery #112 | January 1965 | Thor vs the Hulk |

## Collecting

Journey into Mystery #83 is one of the scarcest of the 1962 Marvel debuts in high grade and among the most valuable. Issues #84 and #85 trail it but are significant keys in their own right. The Golden Record reprint of #83 (1966) and later facsimiles exist; check the indicia.

In the store: [Journey into Mystery #84](/store/journey-into-mystery-84-cgc-6-0) and [Journey into Mystery Annual #1](/store/journey-into-mystery-annual-1-cgc-8-5). The [Thor character page](/characters/thor) lists everything current.

title: What is the first appearance of Iron Man?
answer: Iron Man first appeared in Tales of Suspense #39, cover-dated March 1963, in a story plotted by Stan Lee, scripted by Larry Lieber, drawn by Don Heck, with a cover by Jack Kirby. Tony Stark builds the first, grey armour to escape captivity in Vietnam. The armour turned gold in #40 and became the familiar red and gold in #48 (December 1963), designed by Steve Ditko.
body:
## The debut

Tales of Suspense was a science-fiction anthology. Issue #39's 13-page lead story, "Iron Man Is Born!", gives Stark the chest wound, the arc-lit chestplate and the bulky grey suit. Heck's Stark is a Howard Hughes-style industrialist; Kirby's cover shows the grey armour bursting through a wall.

## The armour changes

- **#39** — grey armour.
- **#40** (April 1963) — gold armour, after a character remarks the grey suit is frightening.
- **#48** (December 1963) — the red-and-gold armour by Ditko, the design that defined the character.

The Iron Man feature shared Tales of Suspense with Captain America from #59 (November 1964), and the title became Captain America with #100; Iron Man moved to his own book with Iron Man #1 in May 1968.

## Collecting Tales of Suspense #39

A major Silver Age key whose demand rose steeply after the 2008 film and has stayed high. High-grade copies are scarce and expensive; mid-grade copies such as the [CGC 6.5 in the store](/store/tales-of-suspense-39-cgc-6-5) are how most collectors own it. Marvel Milestone and facsimile reprints exist.

## Other Iron Man keys

- **Tales of Suspense #52** (April 1964) — first Black Widow.
- **Tales of Suspense #57** (September 1964) — first Hawkeye.
- **Iron Man #55** (February 1973) — first Thanos.
- **Invincible Iron Man #9** (May 2016) — first full appearance of Riri Williams. See [First appearance of Riri Williams](/guides/first-appearance-of-riri-williams).

The [Iron Man character page](/characters/iron-man) lists current stock.

title: What is the first appearance of Doctor Strange?
answer: Doctor Strange first appeared in Strange Tales #110, cover-dated July 1963, in a five-page backup story by Stan Lee and Steve Ditko. The story also introduced Nightmare and the Ancient One. The feature grew into a full series within Strange Tales; the title was renamed Doctor Strange with issue #169 in June 1968.
body:
## The debut

Doctor Strange arrived quietly: five pages at the back of a Human Torch anthology, without a cover mention. Ditko designed the character and the dream dimensions that made the strip famous; Lee's dialogue supplied the incantations. Strange's origin was not told until Strange Tales #115 (December 1963).

## Early Doctor Strange keys

| Issue | Cover date | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Strange Tales #110 | July 1963 | First Doctor Strange, Nightmare, the Ancient One |
| Strange Tales #111 | August 1963 | First Baron Mordo |
| Strange Tales #114 | November 1963 | Captain America try-out story (an impostor), testing demand before Avengers #4 |
| Strange Tales #115 | December 1963 | Origin of Doctor Strange |
| Strange Tales #126 | November 1964 | First Dormammu and Clea |
| Strange Tales #135 | August 1965 | Nick Fury joins the title: first S.H.I.E.L.D. and Hydra |

## Collecting Strange Tales #110

Because Strange is only a backup, the issue was overlooked for decades and was a modest key until the 2016 film. It is now a significant Silver Age book, with the same scarcity in high grade as other 1963 Marvels. A [CBCS 5.0 copy is in the store](/store/strange-tales-110-cbcs-5-0), as is [Strange Tales #135](/store/strange-tales-135-cgc-7-0).

See the [Doctor Strange character page](/characters/doctor-strange) and [Strange Tales #135 and the first S.H.I.E.L.D.](/guides/strange-tales-135-first-shield).

title: What is the first appearance of the X-Men?
answer: The X-Men first appeared in The X-Men #1, cover-dated September 1963, created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby. The issue introduced Professor X and the original five — Cyclops, Marvel Girl (Jean Grey), Beast, Angel and Iceman — and their first enemy, Magneto. It shares its cover date with Avengers #1, published the same month.
body:
## The issue

Lee's premise — mutants born with powers, a school, a war between two philosophies of mutant-kind — is all in the first issue, along with Magneto's attack on the Cape Citadel missile base. Kirby drew the first eleven issues (with layouts after that), and the book found its footing slowly; it was reduced to reprints between #67 and #93 before the 1975 relaunch.

## Original-team keys in the store

- **X-Men #1** (September 1963) — first X-Men and Magneto. Copies in [CGC 4.5](/store/x-men-1-cgc-4-5) and [CBCS 0.5](/store/x-men-1-cbcs-0-5) show how far the price range runs.
- **X-Men #4** (March 1964) — first Scarlet Witch, Quicksilver and the Brotherhood of Evil Mutants.
- **X-Men #9** (January 1965) — first meeting of the X-Men and Avengers; first Lucifer. [In the store](/store/x-men-9-cgc-4-0).
- **X-Men #12** (July 1965) — first Juggernaut.
- **X-Men #14** (November 1965) — first Sentinels.

## The 1975 relaunch

Giant-Size X-Men #1 (May 1975) and X-Men #94 (August 1975) introduced the new team — Storm, Nightcrawler, Colossus, Thunderbird, with Wolverine — and began the Claremont era that made the X-Men Marvel's best-selling franchise. See [Giant-Size X-Men #1 vs X-Men #94](/guides/giant-size-x-men-1-vs-x-men-94) and [First appearance of Storm](/guides/first-appearance-of-storm).

## Collecting X-Men #1

A top Silver Age key, scarce in high grade and often restored. Low-grade copies are still valuable because the demand is deep. Reprints include Marvel Milestone Edition (1991) and facsimiles.

The [X-Men character page](/characters/x-men) lists everything current.

title: What is the first appearance of the Avengers?
answer: The Avengers first appeared in The Avengers #1, cover-dated September 1963, by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby. The founding line-up was Iron Man, Thor, Ant-Man, the Wasp and the Hulk, brought together against Loki. Captain America joined in Avengers #4 (March 1964), which was also his first Silver Age appearance.
body:
## The issue

Unlike the Fantastic Four or X-Men, the Avengers were assembled from heroes who already had their own features, which is why the first issue needs no origins — just Loki's scheme to trap Thor and the Hulk being blamed for a train wreck. The Hulk quit in #2.

## Avengers keys in the store

| Issue | Cover date | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| [Avengers #1](/store/avengers-1-cgc-3-5) | September 1963 | First appearance and formation |
| [Avengers #4](/store/avengers-4-cgc-6-5) | March 1964 | Captain America joins; first Silver Age Cap |
| [Avengers #48](/store/avengers-48-cgc-8-5) | January 1968 | First Dane Whitman as the Black Knight |
| [Avengers #57](/store/avengers-57-cgc-9-4) | October 1968 | First Vision |
| [Avengers #87](/store/avengers-87-cgc-9-8) | April 1971 | Origin of the Black Panther |
| [Avengers #100](/store/avengers-100-cgc-9-8) | June 1972 | Every Avenger to date assembles; Barry Windsor-Smith art |

## Other early keys

- **Avengers #8** (September 1964) — first Kang the Conqueror.
- **Avengers #16** (May 1965) — the new line-up of Captain America, Hawkeye, Quicksilver and Scarlet Witch.
- **Avengers #52** (May 1968) — Black Panther joins.

## Collecting Avengers #1

A first-rank Silver Age key. High-grade copies are scarce; mid- and low-grade copies are the norm. It was reprinted in Marvel Milestone Edition (1993) and as a facsimile.

See the [Avengers character page](/characters/avengers), and [Avengers #4 explained](/guides/avengers-4-captain-america-returns) and [First appearance of the Vision](/guides/first-appearance-of-vision) for two of the keys above.

title: What is the first appearance of Nick Fury?
answer: Nick Fury first appeared in Sgt. Fury and His Howling Commandos #1, cover-dated May 1963, a Second World War combat series by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby. His modern-day identity as an agent of S.H.I.E.L.D. began in Strange Tales #135 (August 1965), which is also the first appearance of S.H.I.E.L.D. and Hydra. Collectors treat both issues as Fury keys for different reasons.
body:
## Sgt. Fury #1

Lee and Kirby's war comic introduced Sergeant Fury and his squad — Dum Dum Dugan, Gabe Jones, Izzy Cohen, Dino Manelli, Reb Ralston and Junior Juniper — fighting in Europe. Lee later said the title was launched partly to prove Marvel's style could sell any genre. Gabe Jones was one of the first Black characters in a regular lead role in a mainstream comic.

## Strange Tales #135

Two years later, Fury was reintroduced as a present-day spy chief in the first half of Strange Tales. Kirby's story introduced S.H.I.E.L.D., its Helicarrier, the Life Model Decoy and Hydra in a single issue. The feature ran until Strange Tales #168 and then in Nick Fury, Agent of S.H.I.E.L.D. #1 (June 1968), the series famous for Jim Steranko's art.

## Which is the key?

- **Sgt. Fury #1** is the true first appearance and the scarcer book in high grade.
- **Strange Tales #135** is the first S.H.I.E.L.D. and the one the film audience knows; its price has risen with the character's screen role.

Both are in the store: [Sgt. Fury #1 CGC 4.0](/store/sgt-fury-and-his-howling-commandos-1-cgc-4-0) and [Strange Tales #135 CGC 7.0](/store/strange-tales-135-cgc-7-0). See also [Strange Tales #135 and the first S.H.I.E.L.D.](/guides/strange-tales-135-first-shield) and the [Nick Fury character page](/characters/nick-fury).
titles: Sgt. Fury and His Howling Commandos

title: What is the first appearance of the Silver Surfer?
answer: The Silver Surfer first appeared in Fantastic Four #48, cover-dated March 1966, the first part of the Galactus Trilogy by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby; Galactus makes his first (partial) appearance in the same issue. Kirby added the Surfer to the story unasked, as a herald for Galactus. The Surfer's own series began with Silver Surfer #1 in August 1968, with art by John Buscema.
body:
## Fantastic Four #48

The Galactus Trilogy (#48–50) is the high point of the Lee–Kirby run. The Surfer appears on the last pages of #48, Galactus fully in #49, and the Surfer's rebellion and exile to Earth close #50. Lee later said he did not know who the silver figure was when Kirby's pages arrived.

## The 1968 series

Silver Surfer #1 (August 1968) was an oversized 25-cent book with a 39-page origin by Lee and Buscema — Norrin Radd of Zenn-La — plus a Watcher backup. The series ran 18 issues to September 1970; Kirby drew the last. It is one of the most collected Silver Age runs because every issue is a Lee–Buscema story and the run is short enough to complete.

| Issue | Cover date | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Silver Surfer #1 | August 1968 | Origin; first issue |
| Silver Surfer #3 | December 1968 | First appearance of Mephisto |
| Silver Surfer #4 | February 1969 | Thor cover; considered the scarcest issue of the run |
| Silver Surfer #14 | March 1970 | Spider-Man crossover |
| Silver Surfer #18 | September 1970 | Last issue; Kirby art |

## In the store

The run is well represented: [#1 CGC 6.5](/store/silver-surfer-1-cgc-6-5), [#1 CGC 6.0](/store/silver-surfer-1-cgc-6-0), [#1 CBCS 8.5 with a verified signature](/store/silver-surfer-1-cbcs-8-5), [#3 CGC 8.0](/store/silver-surfer-3-cgc-8-0), [#3 CGC 8.5](/store/silver-surfer-3-cgc-8-5) and [#4 CGC 8.0](/store/silver-surfer-4-cgc-8-0). See [Silver Surfer (1968): collecting the run](/guides/silver-surfer-1968-collecting-the-run), [First appearance of Mephisto](/guides/first-appearance-of-mephisto) and the [Silver Surfer character page](/characters/silver-surfer).

title: What is the first appearance of Black Panther?
answer: The Black Panther, T'Challa of Wakanda, first appeared in Fantastic Four #52, cover-dated July 1966, by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby, and his origin was told in #53. He was the first Black superhero in mainstream American comics. He joined the Avengers in Avengers #52 (May 1968), his origin was retold in Avengers #87 (April 1971), and his first solo feature ran in Jungle Action from #5 (July 1973).
body:
## Fantastic Four #52

The Panther invites the Fantastic Four to Wakanda and defeats them one by one as a test. Kirby's design — the full-face mask, the technologically advanced African kingdom — was complete from the first issue. Issue #53 gives the origin, the vibranium mound and Ulysses Klaw.

## Key appearances

| Issue | Cover date | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Fantastic Four #52 | July 1966 | First appearance |
| Fantastic Four #53 | August 1966 | Origin; first Klaw |
| Avengers #52 | May 1968 | Joins the Avengers |
| Avengers #87 | April 1971 | Origin retold; in the store as a [CGC 9.8](/store/avengers-87-cgc-9-8) |
| Jungle Action #5 | July 1973 | First solo feature (a reprint of Avengers #62); #6 begins Don McGregor's "Panther's Rage" |
| Black Panther #1 | January 1977 | First solo title, by Kirby |

## Collecting Fantastic Four #52

Demand rose sharply with the 2018 film and has remained strong. High-grade copies are scarce, and the issue is a frequent target for restoration; buy graded. See the [Black Panther character page](/characters/black-panther) and the [Fantastic Four character page](/characters/fantastic-four).

title: What is the first appearance of the Vision?
answer: The Vision first appeared in The Avengers #57, cover-dated October 1968, by Roy Thomas and John Buscema, created by Ultron to destroy the Avengers and joining them by the end of the story. He is not the first Marvel character with the name: a Golden Age Vision, the alien Aarkus, debuted in Marvel Mystery Comics #13 (November 1940) by Joe Simon and Jack Kirby.
body:
## Avengers #57

Thomas revived the Vision name for an android built by Ultron (whose own first full appearance is #55). Buscema's cover — the Vision looming over the fallen Avengers in a red and green costume — is one of the era's most reproduced. The story ends with the famous panel of the Vision weeping, captioned "even an android can cry". Issue #58 tells his origin and makes him a member.

## Why it matters now

The Vision's screen role since 2015 turned a moderately priced Silver Age book into a significant key. High-grade copies carry a steep premium; a [CGC 9.4 is in the store](/store/avengers-57-cgc-9-4).

## Related keys

- **Avengers #54–55** (July–August 1968) — first Ultron (cameo and full).
- **Avengers #58** (November 1968) — origin of the Vision.
- **Marvel Mystery Comics #13** (November 1940) — the Golden Age Vision.

See the [Vision character page](/characters/vision) and [First appearance of the Avengers](/guides/first-appearance-of-avengers).

title: What is the first appearance of Mephisto?
answer: Mephisto first appeared in Silver Surfer #3, cover-dated December 1968, by Stan Lee and John Buscema, tempting the exiled Surfer with a return to Zenn-La and his beloved Shalla-Bal. The issue is the most valuable in the 1968 Silver Surfer run after #1, and demand grew sharply in the early 2020s on speculation about the character's screen debut.
body:
## The issue

Lee wrote Mephisto as a devil figure with the name of Faust's tempter; Buscema's design — red, horned, robed — has barely changed since. The 39-page story is the Surfer's first meeting with him, and the two became recurring antagonists through the run.

## Collecting

Silver Surfer #3 was a modest book until the character's appearances in comics tied to major storylines and talk of a film role turned it into a Silver Age key. High grades are scarce because the 25-cent square-bound format of the early issues chips and stresses easily at the spine. Two copies are in the store: [CGC 8.0](/store/silver-surfer-3-cgc-8-0) and [CGC 8.5](/store/silver-surfer-3-cgc-8-5).

## Other Mephisto appearances of note

- **Silver Surfer #8–9** (1969) — his return.
- **Amazing Spider-Man #545** (January 2008) — "One More Day", the deal that erased the Parker marriage.

See the [Mephisto character page](/characters/mephisto) and [Silver Surfer (1968): collecting the run](/guides/silver-surfer-1968-collecting-the-run).

title: What is the first appearance of Morbius?
answer: Morbius, the Living Vampire, first appeared in The Amazing Spider-Man #101, cover-dated October 1971, by Roy Thomas and Gil Kane; his origin is told in #102. The story is the six-armed Spider-Man arc, and #101 was the first issue of Amazing Spider-Man not written by Stan Lee. Morbius was created as a scientific vampire to get around the Comics Code's ban on the supernatural kind.
body:
## The six-armed saga

Amazing Spider-Man #100 ends with Peter Parker growing four extra arms. In #101 he retreats to a Long Island laboratory where he meets Michael Morbius, a Nobel-winning biochemist whose cure for his own blood disease turned him into a pseudo-vampire. Issue #102, a giant-size 25-cent issue with the Lizard, tells Morbius's origin and resolves the arms.

Thomas made Morbius a scientific rather than supernatural vampire. The Comics Code's 1971 revision, which allowed traditional vampires when handled in the classic literary tradition, opened the door for Tomb of Dracula the following year.

## Collecting

- **#101** is the first appearance and the more valuable book.
- **#102** is the origin, and as a square-bound giant it is hard to find in high grade; a [CGC 9.4 is in the store](/store/amazing-spider-man-102-cgc-9-4).

Both rose with the 2022 film. See the [Morbius character page](/characters/morbius) and [First appearance of Spider-Man](/guides/first-appearance-of-spider-man).

title: What is the first appearance of Ghost Rider?
answer: The Johnny Blaze Ghost Rider first appeared in Marvel Spotlight #5, cover-dated August 1972, created by Roy Thomas, Gary Friedrich and Mike Ploog. The stunt rider who sells his soul to save his mentor and becomes a flaming-skulled spirit of vengeance was an immediate success, and Ghost Rider #1 followed in September 1973. An earlier, unrelated Western character called Ghost Rider appeared at Magazine Enterprises in 1949 and at Marvel in 1967.
body:
## Marvel Spotlight #5

Marvel Spotlight was a try-out title. Issue #5 gave the Ghost Rider his origin in one story: Johnny Blaze, Crash Simpson's carnival cycle show, the bargain with Satan and the transformation. Ploog's cover — the skull-faced rider on a flaming motorcycle — is among the most recognisable of the decade. The character carried Spotlight through #11 before getting his own title.

## Collecting

Marvel Spotlight #5 is one of the top Bronze Age keys, in the same tier as the Punisher's and Moon Knight's debuts, with demand sustained by the films and by the character's place in Marvel's 1970s horror line. High grades are scarce because the black cover shows every scuff. A [CGC 7.5 is in the store](/store/marvel-spotlight-5-cgc-7-5).

## Related

- **Marvel Spotlight #2** (February 1972) — first Werewolf by Night, the book that launched Marvel's horror revival.
- **Ghost Rider #1** (September 1973) — first issue of the solo title.
- **Ghost Rider (vol. 2) #1** (May 1990) — first Danny Ketch, the second Ghost Rider.

See the [Ghost Rider character page](/characters/ghost-rider) and [Bronze Age horror: how the Code change created Tomb of Dracula and Werewolf by Night](/guides/bronze-age-horror-revival).

title: What is the first appearance of Blade?
answer: Blade first appeared in The Tomb of Dracula #10, cover-dated July 1973, created by writer Marv Wolfman and artist Gene Colan as a vampire hunter with wooden knives and a grudge against Dracula. The character's 1998 film made the issue a major Bronze Age key, and demand has stayed high since.
body:
## Tomb of Dracula #10

Tomb of Dracula had begun in April 1972, with Wolfman taking over as writer from #7 and beginning the long run with Colan that made the title the best of Marvel's horror line. Blade arrives in #10 already fully formed — the leather jacket, the goggles, the teak knives — hunting Dracula through London. He became a regular supporting character and later got his own features in the black-and-white magazines.

## Collecting

The issue is scarce in high grade, as most Tomb of Dracula issues are; the dark covers show wear. Blade's later solo keys are minor beside #10. A [CGC 8.0 is in the store](/store/tomb-of-dracula-10-cgc-8-0).

## Tomb of Dracula keys

| Issue | Cover date | Why |
|---|---|---|
| #1 | April 1972 | First Marvel Dracula series; Neal Adams cover |
| #10 | July 1973 | First Blade |
| #12 | September 1973 | Second Blade appearance |
| #25 | October 1974 | First Hannibal King |

See the [Blade character page](/characters/blade) and [Bronze Age horror revival](/guides/bronze-age-horror-revival).

title: What is the first appearance of the Punisher?
answer: The Punisher first appeared in The Amazing Spider-Man #129, cover-dated February 1974, created by writer Gerry Conway with artists Ross Andru and John Romita Sr., who designed the skull costume. The issue also introduced the Jackal. Hired to kill Spider-Man, the Punisher was intended as a one-off antagonist and became one of Marvel's most popular characters.
body:
## The issue

Conway wrote the Punisher as a vigilante manipulated by the Jackal into targeting Spider-Man; the two fight to a draw and the Punisher leaves suspecting he was used. Romita's skull design and Andru's action carried it. The character returned in #134–135, #161–162 and #174–175, then in Daredevil under Frank Miller, and finally in his own limited series in 1986.

## Collecting Amazing Spider-Man #129

One of the three headline Bronze Age keys with Incredible Hulk #181 and Giant-Size X-Men #1. Points to check:

- **Marvel Value Stamp** — the issue contains one, and many copies have it cut out; see [What are Marvel Value Stamps?](/guides/what-are-marvel-value-stamps).
- **Reprints** — Marvel has reissued it several times, including as a facsimile.
- **Grade** — 9.8 copies command a very large premium over 9.4s.

A [CBCS 8.5 copy is in the store](/store/amazing-spider-man-129-cbcs-8-5). See the [Punisher character page](/characters/punisher) and [Why is Amazing Spider-Man #129 a key?](/guides/amazing-spider-man-129-first-punisher).

title: What is the first appearance of Wolverine?
answer: Wolverine's first full appearance is The Incredible Hulk #181, cover-dated November 1974, by Len Wein and Herb Trimpe, with the costume designed by John Romita Sr. He is seen first in a one-panel cameo on the last page of Incredible Hulk #180 (October 1974). Hulk #181 is the most valuable comic of the Bronze Age.
body:
## #180 and #181

Hulk #180 ends with Wolverine bursting in as "Weapon X", sent by the Canadian government to stop the Hulk. Issue #181 is the full three-way fight between Wolverine, the Hulk and the Wendigo. Wein wrote the character as a short, feral Canadian with claws; the healing factor and the rest came later, mostly under Chris Claremont in X-Men.

## Why #181 is the Bronze Age's biggest key

Wolverine became the most popular character of the 1980s and 1990s and a screen franchise since 2000. The issue was printed in normal numbers for 1974, but demand is far beyond any other Bronze Age book, and high-grade copies are further reduced by the Marvel Value Stamp: many copies have the stamp cut from an interior page and receive a green qualified label. See [What are Marvel Value Stamps?](/guides/what-are-marvel-value-stamps).

## What to check when buying

1. **Stamp intact** — on the label notes or confirmed by the seller.
2. **Label colour** — restored copies are common because the book is worth restoring; a [CBCS 2.0 restored copy in the store](/store/incredible-hulk-181-cbcs-2-0-restored) shows how the market prices one.
3. **Reprints** — Marvel has reprinted #181 many times, including facsimiles.

An unrestored [CGC 3.5 is in the store](/store/incredible-hulk-181-cgc-3-5).

## Wolverine's next keys

- **Giant-Size X-Men #1** (May 1975) — joins the new X-Men.
- **X-Men #94** (August 1975) — first regular issue of the new team; [copies in the store](/store/x-men-94-cgc-9-2).
- **Wolverine #1** (September 1982) — the Claremont–Miller limited series.

See [Why is Incredible Hulk #181 so valuable?](/guides/incredible-hulk-181-first-wolverine) and the [Wolverine character page](/characters/wolverine).

title: What is the first appearance of Moon Knight?
answer: Moon Knight first appeared in Werewolf by Night #32, cover-dated August 1975, created by writer Doug Moench and artist Don Perlin as a silver-clad mercenary hired to capture the werewolf Jack Russell. He returned in #33, was given his own backup and try-out stories, and starred in Moon Knight #1 in November 1980 with Moench and Bill Sienkiewicz.
body:
## Werewolf by Night #32

The issue is a two-parter with #33: the Committee hires Marc Spector to bring in the werewolf, and the silver costume and crescent darts are explained by the target. Moench's Moon Knight was an antagonist first; the Egyptian god Khonshu, the multiple identities and the rest were built in Marvel Spotlight #28–29 (1976) and the 1980 series.

## Collecting

Werewolf by Night #32 was a mid-tier Bronze Age key for decades and moved into the top tier with the 2022 series. It contains a Marvel Value Stamp; check that it is intact. A [CGC 7.5 is in the store](/store/werewolf-by-night-32-cgc-7-5).

## Related keys

- **Werewolf by Night #33** (September 1975) — second appearance, concluding the story.
- **Marvel Spotlight #28** (June 1976) — first solo story.
- **Moon Knight #1** (November 1980) — first issue of his own title; origin.

See the [Moon Knight character page](/characters/moon-knight) and [Bronze Age horror revival](/guides/bronze-age-horror-revival).

title: What is the first appearance of Storm? Giant-Size X-Men #1 explained
answer: Storm first appeared in Giant-Size X-Men #1, cover-dated May 1975, by Len Wein and Dave Cockrum — the issue that also introduced Nightcrawler, Colossus and Thunderbird and brought Wolverine, Banshee and Sunfire together as the new X-Men. The regular series resumed with X-Men #94 (August 1975), which began Chris Claremont's sixteen-year run as writer.
body:
## Giant-Size X-Men #1

The X-Men title had been in reprints since #67. Wein and Cockrum's 68-page relaunch has Professor X recruiting an international team to rescue the original X-Men from the living island Krakoa. Cockrum's cover, the new team bursting through a picture of the old one, is one of the most homaged images in comics. Ororo Munroe, worshipped as a goddess in Kenya, is recruited in the opening pages.

## Who debuts where

| Character | First appearance |
|---|---|
| Storm, Nightcrawler, Colossus, Thunderbird | Giant-Size X-Men #1 (May 1975) |
| Wolverine | Incredible Hulk #181 (November 1974) — joins the team here |
| Banshee | X-Men #28 (January 1967) |
| Sunfire | X-Men #64 (January 1970) |

## Collecting

Giant-Size X-Men #1 is one of the three headline Bronze Age keys with Incredible Hulk #181 and Amazing Spider-Man #129. Its square-bound spine chips easily, so high grades are scarce. It contains a Marvel Value Stamp. X-Men #94, the first regular issue, is the companion key and is in the store in several grades: [CGC 9.2](/store/x-men-94-cgc-9-2), [CGC 9.2 off-white pages](/store/x-men-94-cgc-9-2-off-white) and [CGC 8.0](/store/x-men-94-cgc-8-0).

See [Giant-Size X-Men #1 vs X-Men #94: which is the key?](/guides/giant-size-x-men-1-vs-x-men-94), the [Storm character page](/characters/storm) and the [X-Men character page](/characters/x-men).

title: What is the first appearance of Nova?
answer: Nova — Richard Rider, the teenager who inherits the power of a dying Nova Corps centurion — first appeared in Nova #1, cover-dated September 1976, created by Marv Wolfman and John Buscema for Marvel. The series was Marvel's deliberate attempt at a new Spider-Man-style teen hero and ran 25 issues to 1979.
body:
## Nova #1

Wolfman had created a version of the character for a fanzine years earlier and reworked him for Marvel. The first issue is a complete origin: the alien Rhomann Dey, the transfer of power, the helmet and the flight. Buscema drew the first issues; the cover blurb promised "in the marvellous tradition of Spider-Man".

## Collecting

Nova #1 is a Bronze Age key whose demand has tracked the character's prominence in cosmic Marvel stories and film rumours. High-grade copies are reasonably available compared with 1974–1975 keys, so the premium is concentrated at 9.8. A [CBCS 9.8 is in the store](/store/nova-1-cbcs-9-8).

## Related

- **Nova #25** (May 1979) — last issue of the original run.
- **New Warriors #1** (July 1990) — Nova's return as part of the team.
- **Annihilation: Nova #1** (2006) — the reinvention that made the character central to Marvel's cosmic line.

See the [Nova character page](/characters/nova) and the [Bronze Age collection](/collections/bronze-age).

title: What is the first appearance of Phoenix?
answer: Jean Grey became Phoenix in The X-Men #101, cover-dated October 1976, by Chris Claremont and Dave Cockrum, rising from Jamaica Bay after piloting a shuttle through a solar flare. Jean herself first appeared as Marvel Girl in X-Men #1 (September 1963); #101 is the first appearance of the Phoenix identity and costume. The Dark Phoenix Saga followed in X-Men #129–137 (1980).
body:
## X-Men #101

The issue closes the Sentinels story begun in #98 and opens with the shuttle crash. Cockrum's cover of Phoenix erupting from the water in the green-and-gold costume is one of the defining X-Men images. The story also takes the team to Banshee's castle in Ireland, setting up Juggernaut and Black Tom.

## Phoenix keys

| Issue | Cover date | Why |
|---|---|---|
| X-Men #1 | September 1963 | First Jean Grey |
| X-Men #101 | October 1976 | First Phoenix |
| X-Men #129 | January 1980 | Start of the Dark Phoenix Saga; first Kitty Pryde and Emma Frost |
| X-Men #134 | June 1980 | First Dark Phoenix |
| X-Men #135 | July 1980 | Dark Phoenix cover |
| X-Men #137 | September 1980 | Death of Phoenix |

## Collecting

X-Men #101 is one of the most collected Claremont-era issues; a [CGC 9.8 is in the store](/store/x-men-101-cgc-9-8), alongside [X-Men #129 in 9.8](/store/x-men-129-cgc-9-8). See the [Phoenix character page](/characters/phoenix), [First appearance of Kitty Pryde](/guides/first-appearance-of-kitty-pryde) and the [X-Men character page](/characters/x-men).

title: What is the first appearance of Kitty Pryde?
answer: Kitty Pryde first appeared in The X-Men #129, cover-dated January 1980, by Chris Claremont and John Byrne, as a thirteen-year-old from Deerfield, Illinois recruited by Professor X. The same issue introduced Emma Frost (the White Queen) and Sebastian Shaw of the Hellfire Club and began the Dark Phoenix Saga, which makes it one of the most important issues of the Claremont–Byrne run.
body:
## X-Men #129

Byrne based Kitty partly on a real teenager he knew; her phasing power and her ordinariness made her the reader's viewpoint on the team for years. The issue's second half introduces the Hellfire Club's inner circle, and the story runs without a break through #137 and the death of Phoenix.

## Why #129 is a key three times over

1. First Kitty Pryde (Shadowcat).
2. First Emma Frost, one of the most prominent X-Men characters since the 2000s.
3. First Sebastian Shaw and the start of the Dark Phoenix Saga.

## Collecting

As a 1980 book with a large print run, #129 survives in quantity and the market is concentrated at 9.6 and 9.8; a [CGC 9.8 is in the store](/store/x-men-129-cgc-9-8). Newsstand copies carry a small premium. See [First appearance of Phoenix](/guides/first-appearance-of-phoenix), the [Kitty Pryde character page](/characters/kitty-pryde) and the [X-Men character page](/characters/x-men).

title: What is the first appearance of She-Hulk?
answer: She-Hulk first appeared in The Savage She-Hulk #1, cover-dated February 1980, written by Stan Lee and drawn by John Buscema — one of the last characters Lee created for Marvel. Jennifer Walters, Bruce Banner's cousin, receives a transfusion of his blood after a shooting. Marvel created the character partly to secure the trademark before a television spin-off of The Incredible Hulk could.
body:
## Savage She-Hulk #1

Lee wrote only the first issue; David Anthony Kraft took over with #2 and wrote the rest of the 25-issue run, which ended in 1982. Buscema's cover shows the green She-Hulk towering over Jennifer's image. The character was reinvented by John Byrne in Sensational She-Hulk (1989) as a comedic, fourth-wall-breaking lead.

## Collecting

The book was inexpensive for decades and rose with the 2022 series. Because it is a 1980 book, supply is ample and the value sits in 9.8 copies; a [CGC 9.8 is in the store](/store/savage-she-hulk-1-cgc-9-8). Check for newsstand copies, which are scarcer in high grade.

## Related keys

- **Incredible Hulk #1** (May 1962) — see [First appearance of the Hulk](/guides/first-appearance-of-hulk).
- **Sensational She-Hulk #1** (May 1989) — Byrne's relaunch.

See the [She-Hulk character page](/characters/she-hulk).

title: What is the first appearance of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles?
answer: The Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles first appeared in Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles #1, cover-dated May 1984, self-published by Kevin Eastman and Peter Laird as Mirage Studios in Dover, New Hampshire. The first printing was a black-and-white, magazine-sized comic of about 3,000 copies. Later printings from 1984 and 1985 look similar but are clearly marked, and only the first printing carries the high value.
body:
## The book

Eastman and Laird financed the first printing with a tax refund and a loan, printed roughly 3,000 copies, and advertised it in the Comic Buyer's Guide. The story is a parody of Frank Miller's Daredevil and Ronin — the ooze, the ninja clan, the gritty New York — played straight enough to work. The characters became a global franchise within three years.

## Identifying the first printing

| Printing | Date | How to tell |
|---|---|---|
| First | May 1984 | No printing statement in the indicia; approximately 3,000 copies |
| Second | June 1984 | "Second printing" stated; about 6,000 copies |
| Third | February 1985 | Stated; larger run |
| Fourth and later | 1985 onward | Stated; some with colour or different covers |

Always read the indicia. The first printing is one of the most counterfeited independent comics; grade or authenticate before buying.

## Collecting

A first-printing TMNT #1 is the most valuable Copper Age comic and among the most valuable independents ever published. Later printings are affordable and collectible in their own right — the copy in the store is a [1985 printing in CGC 9.6 with a witnessed signature](/store/teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles-1-cgc-9-6), listed with its printing stated.

## Related keys

- **TMNT #2** (October 1984) — first printing about 15,000 copies.
- **Raphael #1** (1985) — first Casey Jones.

See the [Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles character page](/characters/teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles), the [Mirage Studios publisher page](/publishers/mirage-studios) and [TMNT #1 printings explained](/guides/tmnt-1-printings-explained).

title: What is the first appearance of John Constantine?
answer: John Constantine's first full appearance is The Saga of the Swamp Thing #37, cover-dated June 1985, by Alan Moore, Stephen Bissette and John Totleben, who modelled his look on the musician Sting. He can be glimpsed in background cameos in Saga of the Swamp Thing #25 (June 1984). Constantine's own series, Hellblazer, began in January 1988 and ran 300 issues.
body:
## Saga of the Swamp Thing #37

Moore's run on Swamp Thing (from #20, January 1984) had already redefined the character. Issue #37 begins the "American Gothic" arc: a trench-coated Liverpudlian occultist turns up to recruit Swamp Thing for a tour of American horrors, chain-smoking and refusing to explain himself. Bissette and Totleben had drawn a Sting lookalike into #25 as a joke; Moore built the character around him.

## Collecting

Saga of the Swamp Thing #37 is the most valuable issue of the run and a top Copper Age key, helped by the 2005 and 2014 screen versions. As a 1985 direct-market book it survives in high grade, so the market is concentrated at 9.6 and 9.8; a [CGC 9.8 is in the store](/store/swamp-thing-37-cgc-9-8). Issue #25 trades at a fraction, as a cameo.

## Related keys

- **Saga of the Swamp Thing #20** (January 1984) — Moore's first issue.
- **Saga of the Swamp Thing #21** (February 1984) — "The Anatomy Lesson".
- **Hellblazer #1** (January 1988) — first issue of his own title, by Jamie Delano and John Ridgway.

See the [John Constantine character page](/characters/john-constantine) and the [DC Comics publisher page](/publishers/dc-comics).

title: What is the first appearance of Deadpool?
answer: Deadpool first appeared in The New Mutants #98, cover-dated February 1991, created by Fabian Nicieza and Rob Liefeld, as a mercenary hired to kill Cable. The same issue introduced Gideon and Domino (revealed later to be the impostor Copycat). It is the most valuable comic of the early 1990s and the standard example of a Modern Age key.
body:
## New Mutants #98

Liefeld was two issues from the end of New Mutants, which became X-Force with #1 in August 1991. Deadpool — the red-and-black costume, the swords, the mouth — was a Liefeld design with Nicieza's dialogue; Nicieza has said the Deathstroke resemblance (Wade Wilson, Slade Wilson) was pointed out to him at the time. Deadpool was a villain here; the comedy came later in Joe Kelly's 1997 series.

## Collecting

New Mutants #98 was printed in large numbers and most copies were bagged at once, so 9.8 copies are plentiful in absolute terms — but demand since the 2016 film dwarfs any other 1990s book. Points to check:

- **Newsstand copies** are scarcer and carry a premium. See [Newsstand vs direct edition](/guides/newsstand-vs-direct-edition).
- **Second printings and facsimiles** exist; read the indicia.
- **Gold and silver reprints** from 1990s promotions are separate items.

A [CGC 9.6 is in the store](/store/new-mutants-98-cgc-9-6). See the [Deadpool character page](/characters/deadpool) and the [Copper Age collection](/collections/copper-age).

title: What is the first appearance of Harley Quinn?
answer: Harley Quinn's first comic-book appearance is The Batman Adventures #12, cover-dated September 1993, by Kelley Puckett, Mike Parobeck and Rick Burchett, in the tie-in series to Batman: The Animated Series. She was created by Paul Dini and Bruce Timm for the television episode “Joker's Favor”, first broadcast in September 1992, a year before she reached print.
body:
## Batman Adventures #12

The Batman Adventures adapted the animated series' style for comics. Issue #12, "Batgirl: Day One", has Harley and Poison Ivy teaming up against Batgirl, with Harley in her original red-and-black jester costume. The Parobeck cover of the trio is the image collectors want.

## Why it is a key

Harley went from a one-episode henchwoman to one of DC's most published characters and a film lead. Batman Adventures #12 is the first appearance in comics, and the market treats it as her key. Her first appearance in the main DC continuity is Batman: Harley Quinn #1 (October 1999), and the Mad Love one-shot (February 1994) by Dini and Timm tells her origin.

## Collecting

As a 1993 book, supply in high grade is good and the market is a 9.8 market; a [CGC 9.8 is in the store](/store/batman-adventures-12-cgc-9-8). Newsstand copies and the scarcer second printing carry premiums. Beware the 2015 and later reprints and facsimiles.

See the [Harley Quinn character page](/characters/harley-quinn), [Batman Adventures #12 explained](/guides/batman-adventures-12-first-harley-quinn) and the [Modern Age collection](/collections/modern-age).

title: What is the first appearance of Riri Williams (Ironheart)?
answer: Riri Williams' first full appearance is Invincible Iron Man #9, cover-dated May 2016, by Brian Michael Bendis and Mike Deodato, after a cameo in Invincible Iron Man #7 (March 2016). The fifteen-year-old MIT student who builds her own armour took the name Ironheart in the relaunched Invincible Iron Man #1, released in November 2016.
body:
## The debut

Bendis introduced Riri reverse-engineering Iron Man armour in her dorm room; #7 shows her at work in a few pages and #9 gives her a proper story, with Tony Stark taking notice. The 2016 series, launched after Civil War II, put her in the lead role with Stark as an AI mentor.

## Which issue is the key?

- **#7** — cameo, first appearance.
- **#9** — first full appearance and the one most collectors treat as the key.
- **Invincible Iron Man #1 (2016)** — first as Ironheart.

See [First appearance vs cameo](/guides/first-appearance-vs-cameo) for why the market splits it this way.

## Collecting

Modern Age keys like this are a 9.8 market; variants of #9 and #7 carry premiums. Demand rose with the character's screen appearances from 2022. A [CGC 9.8 is in the store](/store/invincible-iron-man-9-cgc-9-8). See the [Riri Williams character page](/characters/riri-williams) and [First appearance of Iron Man](/guides/first-appearance-of-iron-man).
